text: Five providers, four-ish tiers each, open-weight or closed — that's a lot of options. This lesson is the actual process for picking one, straight from how a provider itself tells you to decide.

Four questions, before anything else. What capabilities does this task actually need — long context, tool use, vision? How fast does it need to respond — real-time chat versus an overnight batch job are completely different? What's the real budget at production volume, not demo volume? And can you tune effort within one model before switching models entirely — that's often a better first lever than jumping tiers.

Pick one of two strategies, then actually test it. Efficiency-first: start cheap and fast, test against real examples, upgrade only where you find a genuine capability gap. Capability-first: start with the strongest model for a genuinely hard task, then look for room to step down once you understand what it actually needs. Neither one means always reaching for the biggest model.

Three real tasks. A high-volume FAQ chatbot — efficiency-first, fastest tier. Drafting a first-pass document from a messy transcript — moderate complexity, a balanced mid-tier model. A multi-step coding agent refactoring an unfamiliar codebase — capability-first, the flagship tier, with room to downgrade only once the workflow is proven out.

Capabilities, speed, cost, effort — then test against your real data, not a marketing benchmark. Next lesson: what that actually costs, with real numbers across the full cost-latency-quality trade-off.
